newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS- Hoogovens profits up, shares down.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Hoogovens profits up, shares down.

text.p: Dutch metals group Hoogovens NV reported a 40 percent jump in first-half earnings on Wednesday but the company's share price slipped as investors realised headline profits were boosted by one-off gains.

The steel and aluminium producer said net profit rose to 194 million guilders ($91.7 million), from 139 million in the same period of 1996, but this included 13 million guilders of extraordinary income from the sale of various small businesses.
Net profit from normal operations rose some 25 percent to 178 million guilders, a slightly lower figure than the consensus figure of 186 million from a Reuters poll of analysts.
Hoogovens said nascent economic recovery in Europe and favourable conditions elsewhere had led to good demand for its products, allowing it to maintain high sales volumes.

Selling prices for both metals were similar or slightly lower than first-half 1996 levels, but Hoogovens said it had increased profits by further reducing costs and upgrading its product mix by adding more value to its output.

Hoogovens chairman Maarten van Veen was bullish about the outlook for the rest of the year. "The positive performance of the economy will be sustained in the second half of the year, thereby creating room for an increase in prices," he told a news conference.
Van Veen said he expected net profit from normal operations to show a strong increase, and when pressed for detail, said the rise would be at the high end of a range of 20 to 30 percent.

First-half turnover rose 19 percent to 4.50 billion guilders, partly as a result of the acquisition of the remaining 50 percent of German steel-processing firm Hille & Muller and the formation of the Hoogovens Boel joint venture in Belgium.
Van Veen said the additional steel-rolling capacity acquired under the Boel deal had helped to push up the proportion of finished steel products to 93 percent.
In the past Hoogovens had traditionally sold about a fifth of its steel output as semi-finished slabs or billets which were then processed by other companies.

Van Veen said Hoogovens Boel was still losing money for the time being, naming it as one of several business units in steel and aluminium which fell short of Hoogovens' target of an annual average return of 12.5 percent on investment.

Hoogovens' aluminium business also managed to raise its profits even though primary aluminium prices were more or less unchanged from first-half 1996 levels and prices of rolled and extruded aluminium products were actually lower.
This was offset by higher sales volumes and an improved product mix.

The company said the higher dollar had boosted operating profits by several tens of millions of guilders, noting that the dollar effect on selling prices was mitigated by higher prices for raw materials denominated in dollars.

Analysts expressed some reservations about Hoogovens' results which fell short of most of their expectations. "We had thought the result would be more positive than it was, the quality does not look so good but it's a bit early to tell," said Kim Broekhuyse of ING Barings.

On the Amsterdam bourse Hoogovens shares, which have risen much more sharply than the market as a whole this year, closed 3.20 guilders lower at 132.80 after initially sprinting ahead when the company's results first hit dealers' screens.

"They looked good at the start but it's the extraordinary gain. If you strip the 13 million guilders out then they lose their shine. You could even say the results were disappointing," said one dealer. -- Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000, Fax +31 20 504 5040 ($ = 2.114 Dutch Guilders)
